Valorization of rapeseed straw through the enhancement of cellulose accessibility, lignin removal and xylan elimination using an n-alkyltrimethylammonium bromide-based deep eutectic solvent
Zhengyu Tang a,1 , Chaowei Zhang a,1 , Junyao Yin a,1 , Bo Fan a, Yu-Cai He a,*, Cuiluan Ma b,*
ª School of Pharmacy & Biological and Food Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou 213164, China b Key Laboratory of Biocatalysis and Enzyme Engineering, Hubei University, Wuhan 430062, China
ARTICLE INFO --- **Keywords:** * Lignin removal * Lignocellulose * Xylan elimination

ABSTRACT n-Alkyltrimethylammonium bromide (CₙTAB)-based deep eutectic solvent (DESs) has potential in the efficient delignification and utilization of carbohydrates in biomass. In this research, DESs containing Brønsted acid and Lewis acid were prepared with CₙTAB (alkyl-chain length 12–18), organic acids and metal chlorides, and the optimal treatment conditions were acquired by pretreatment optimization. Through the pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) (162.5 °C, 61.7 min), lignin (89.2 %) and xylan (77.9 %) were effectively eliminated, and the hydrophobicity of rapeseed straw substantially declined from 4.62 to 2.09 m²/g, acquiring the highest enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 92.5 %. The relationship of DES properties and enzymatic saccharification efficiency was explored. Additionally, hemicellulose in rapeseed straws could be efficiently transformed into furfural (3.75 g/L) and xylo-oligosaccharides (3.64 g/L). To clarify the structural and property changes brought by pretreatment, rapeseed straws were testified by FT-IR, SEM and CLSM and deeply discussed. The interaction between lignocellulose and TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was elucidated by molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations, explaining the effectual treatment performance and hemicel-lulose upgrading at the molecular level. Eventually, a potential pretreatment mechanism of TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was proposed. This established TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ treatment holds great promise for valorization of biomass into biofuels and biobased chemicals.

1. Introduction In the pursuit of sustainable energy, human society is actively seeking alternatives to fossil fuel consumption [1]. One promising approach is the utilization of lignocellulosic biomass, which is composed of carbohydrates (hemicellulose plus cellulose) and lignin, making it suitable for manufacturing biofuels and chemicals [2,3]. Enzymatic digestion is extensively regarded as the most promising method for utilizing carbohydrates [1]. These lignocellulose-derived reducing sugars can be further upgraded to high value-added chemicals or bio- fuels through fermentation or biocatalysis [4,5]. And these upgraded chemicals include furfural, xylo-oligosaccharides, ethanol, etc., which play an important role in the fields of resin/pharmaceutical in- termediates synthesis, health products production and energy [6]. However, the existence of lignin in lignocellulose poses challenges as

they form barriers around carbohydrates, blocking the enzymatic digestion process [7]. Thus, developing an effectual pretreatment strategy for breaking down the complex structure of lignocellulosic biomass is crucial. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as effective solvents for lignocellulose treatment due to their excellent performance in enhancing enzymatic digestion [8,9]. They are a kind of readily synthesizable solvent with low vapor pressure, which can effectively separate hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. Compared with traditional hydrothermal pretreatment, it avoids the significant investment in high-pressure reactors and is less corrosive to equipment, reducing subsequent maintenance costs [10]. Typically, choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine (BA) are used as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) in DESs [11]. Besides conventional HBAs, alternative HBAs with additional functionalities for pretreatment hold significant potential to further advance pretreatment technology. The cationic surfactant (e.g., n-

alkyltrimethylammonium bromide, CₙTAB) is one such alternative for HBA of DESs [12]. As an additive with good safety and controllable costs, CₙTAB is widely used in the manufacturing of rubber and daily chemical products. Currently, the acidic CTAB:LA pretreatment strategy developed based on CTAB surfactant has shown a remarkable increase in enzyme digestibility by 72% and an improvement in cellulose accessibility from 297 mg/g to 473 mg/g [12]. Pretreatment based on CTAB-based DES has been testified to be highly beneficial as it aids in delignification and prevents the redeposition of pseudo-lignin, thereby improving cellulose accessibility and accelerating cellulose hydrolysis. In addition, the metal salt, as a kind of inexpensive and efficient Lewis acid catalysts, has attracted special attention due to its excellent pretreatment performance [13]. As a Lewis acid catalyst, metal salts can not only catalyze the hydrolysis of β-1,4-glucoside, and β-O-4 bonds in hemicellulose and lignin, but also coordinate with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignin, change their structure and chemical properties, and improve the efficiency of lignin removal. It has been widely reported to accelerate the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass, particularly hemicellulose, and to significantly improve the efficiency of biomass pretreatment. During the bulrush pretreatment, supplementary AlCl₃ could be used to assist ChCl:Gly pretreatment, acquiring high delignification (70.8%), xylan elimination (87.7%), and the saccharification yield (90.1%) [14]. Therefore, it deserves the development of new acidic DESs containing metal ion and surfactant for efficiently improving the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of lignocellulose.

During the pretreatment process in acidic systems, there is also the opportunity to produce high-value products xylo-oligosaccharides (XOSs), and furfural [15], which are both important biobased addi- tives or intermediates in the food and pharmaceutical industries, with high application value [16]. It is recognized that acidic DES containing organic acids can promote the hydrolysis of hemicellulose, leading to the elevated saccharification capacity and acquiring byproducts such as xylose and XOSs. Additionally, metal chlorides, acting as Lewis acids, can favor the degradation of xylose and greatly accelerate the generation of furfural [17,18]. The protons provided by organic acids (such as lactic acid, LCA) can not only promote the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellulose and lignin, but also greatly inhibit the deactivation of metal ions due to hydration. Through the synergistic action of Brønsted acid and Lewis acid, the structure of lignocellulose is effectively disrupted, and enzy- matic hydrolysis is enhanced to obtain a high yield of reducing sugar. Moreover, this synergy facilitates the hydrolysis of xylan and dehydra- tion of xylose, promoting the formation of XOSs and furfural [15]. Supplementary of 0.2 mol/L formic acid into an aqueous system helped achieve the XOSs yield of 68% and enhance biomass saccharification ability (160 °C, 120 min) [19]. Catalyst AT-Sn-YB immobilized with Lewis acid sites (Sn⁴+) was used for the catalytic upgrading of bamboo, resulting in the production of 17.2 g/L fermentable sugars and 2.8 g/L XOSs, with an 80.3% yield of furfural [20]. To accomplish high biomass saccharification and hemicellulose utilization, the organic acid and metal chloride-containing DESs were attempted for the synthesis of XOSs, furfural and reducing sugars.

To well understand the pretreatment mechanism, molecular dy- namics (MD) simulations and quantum chemistry calculations can be applied to analyze the molecular structure of lignocellulose and explore deeply the interaction between the solvent and lignocellulose. Accord- ingly, in order to further investigate the interactions between CₙTAB/ LCA/Fe³⁺ and lignocellulose at the molecular level, MD simulations and quantum chemical calculations can be attempted to deeply interpret the pretreatment mechanism combining with structural characterizations [21].

It is known that rapeseed straw (RS) represents a readily available bioenergy resource that is often disregarded and subjected to disposal or incineration practices [22,23]. It is of great interest to valorize RS into valuable chemicals through the effectual pretreatment. In this study, it was predicted that the CₙTAB-based DES pretreatment would significantly alter the physicochemical characteristics and microstructures of

RS. Additionally, the increased accessibility of cellulose, and weakened hydrophobicity might be beneficial for enzymatic digestion of RS. Correspondingly, an effectual C₁TAB-based DES pretreatment process was established to address the recalcitrance of RS and mitigate the inhibitory effects of lignin and hemicellulose on enzymatic saccharification. In addition, the co-production of XOSs, furfural, and reducing sugars was developed through the efficient pretreatment. Initially, the chain length of C₁TAB (12–18), organic acid type, and metal salt type in C₁TAB-based DESs were systematically screened using single factor analysis, and the response surface method (RSM) was used to optimize the pretreatment conditions and further improve the saccharification effect of cellulose. Afterwards, the synergistic production potential of fermentable sugars, furfural, and XOSs within the pretreatment system was testified, considering factors (such as C₁TAB chain length, and FeCl₃ ratio) and their impact on pretreatment efficiency. Various analytical techniques such as FT-IR, CLSM, and SEM were employed to explore the effect of TTAB/LCA/Fe%+ on the RS morphology and properties. Molecular dynamics simulations were also utilized to gain insights into the changes in biomass properties at a molecular level. These investigations aimed to elucidate the mechanism for underlying the synergistic production and provided valuable information for the development of efficient biomass refining strategies through effectual pretreatment.

China), which was composed of 30.2% of glucan, 15.1% of xylan, 18.9% of lignin, 16.2 % of ash, 5.5% of crude protein and 11.4% of water. The impacts of different C_nTAB, organic acid and metal chloride in DES were examined on the changes of glucose yield and RS components (Fig. 1). Fig. 1a showcased that the glucose yield from biomass didn't increase consistently as the chain length of C_nTAB increased from 12 to 18. It manifested that the tetra- decyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB)-based DES obtained the best pretreatment effectiveness, acquiring an enzymatic digestion efficiency of 64.5 %. As illustrated in Fig. 1e, it could be observed that xylan and lignin in the biomass was significant eliminated as the chain length of C_nTAB decreased, increasing the xylan elimination from 65.5 % to 73.4 % and delignification from 61.8 % to 77.4 % (Table S1, see supple- mentary materials). After pretreatment with DTAB/LCA, the solid re- covery was <40 %, which was the lowest among all the C_nTAB-based DESs tested. It turned out that the DTAB resulted in the most significant structural disruption. However, although the dodecyl- trimethylammonium bromide (DTAB) with the shortest alkyl chains exhibited the most significant structural disruption based on chemical composition, it didn't acquire the best glucose yield. This was likely due to the higher production of inhibitory compounds during the more intense pretreatment process caused by DTAB, thereby limiting the saccharification efficiency of RS [32].

The Brønsted acid in the ternary DES played a crucial role in biomass pretreatment by providing a large number of protons for attacking the chemical bonds in biomass, thus substantially reducing the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials [19]. In this research, four different mono- carboxylic acids with varying chain lengths and two common organic acids (lactic acid and levulinic acid) were individually mixed with the best CₙTAB obtained above, and TTAB-based DESs with different organic acids were screened to acquire the most suitable binary CₙTAB- based DES for RS pretreatment. From Fig. 1f, the RS treated with DES containing lactic acid (LCA) had the lowest lignin content (9.4%). It could be calculated that DES containing LCA effectually eliminated the highest amount of lignin (77.2%) and xylan (69.7%) within the system, followed by the DES with formic acid, reaching 74.9% and 76.8%, respectively. Among these organic acids, butyric acid exhibited the weakest disruption of the lignocellulose structure, which might be

attributed to its relatively higher pKa value. Fig. 1b indicated that the RS pretreatment using CnHAB-based DES containing LCA exhibited the best performance, with an enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 64.5 %. Additionally, it was observed that the elimination capacity of monocarboxylic acids for lignin and xylan gradually weakened with increasing chain length. This trend was closely related to the pKa values, as showcased in Fig. 1b. As the chain length of monocarboxylic acids increased, their pKa values also rose, resulting in a decline in pretreatment efficiency. However, the pKa of acids couldn't be used directly to predict pretreatment results. When organic acids such as lactic acid possess more complex structures, including hydroxyl and carbonyl groups, the correlation between pKa and pretreatment performance couldn't be simply described as negative. On one hand, different functional groups apparently influenced the stereostructure of organic acids, thereby affecting the pretreatment process. On the other hand, complex organic acids might exhibit intramolecular interactions, such as the significant impact of hydroxyl groups on hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic interactions, which would influence the ionization equilibrium of carboxyl groups.

In the pretreatment system, metal chlorides can not only act as Lewis acid to catalyze the hydrolysis of chemical bonds such as β-1,4-glucoside and β-O-4 bonds in hemicelluloses and lignin [33], but also react with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignocellulose to form metal ion-lignin complexes, making them easier to degrade [13]. In Fig. 1c, the pretreatment effectiveness of nine DESs containing different metal chlorides was compared. It was manifested that the ternary DESs containing metal chlorides exhibited apparently improved pretreatment performance compared to TTAB/LCA. The lowest enzymatic digestion efficiency for RS pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Mn²⁺ was 54.3 %, while higher saccharification efficiencies were acquired with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ and TTAB/LCA/Al³⁺ treatments, reaching 83.6 % and 81.5 %, respectively. Considering the comprehensive screening of components in the ternary DES above, TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was considered the optimal CₙTAB-based ternary DES for RS pretreatment.

It is widely recognized that the properties of DESs have substantial impacts on the elimination of biomass components [34]. As shown in the FT-IR image of TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (Fig. S1, see supplementary materials),

a peak due to the stretching vibration of -OH was observed at 3450 cm⁻¹, showing a blue shift compared to LCA, indicating the formation of a new hydrogen bond network in DES [35]. The peak appeared at 1746 cm⁻¹ was associated with C=O in from LCA [36]. A peak at 966 cm⁻¹ was attributed to the C–N group of TTAB and the absorption around 744 cm⁻¹ was connected with Fe³⁺-OH- Fe³⁺ [37]. In biomass pretreatment, solvent viscosity plays a crucial role in the diffusion rate of molecules [34]. There was a substantial difference in viscosity among DESs synthesized using CₙTAB with different chain lengths (Table S2, see supplementary materials). It was evident that DESs synthesized with shorter alkyl chain lengths exhibit lower viscosity. The viscosity of octadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (OTAB) was 1983.5 cp, while that of DTAB was only 350.3 cp. It was probably related to lower intermolecular friction caused by lower chain length, thus resulting in better mobility. This helped the molecules move more easily in the solvent, confirming that TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ had better pretreatment performance. Additionally, at room temperature, ternary DESs showed a significant reduction in viscosity compared to binary DESs. The viscosity of TTAB/LCA reached 848.2 cp, whereas TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ had only 674.2 cp. These findings regarding viscosity were consistent with previous studies on the pretreatment effectiveness of different DESs.

Surface tension is also a crucial solvent property known to influence the pretreatment process. Solvents with low surface tension might better interact with biomass and rapidly penetrate structures such as lignin. The formed stronger interactions would facilitate their efficient removal. TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ had a surface tension of only 30.2 mN/m (Table S2, see supplementary materials). In comparison, the surface tension of water was 72 mN/m (25 °C), significantly higher than that of this efficient pretreatment solvent. Consistent with the viscosity trend, the shorter chain lengths of CₙTAB also contributed to lower surface tension in DESs, thereby promoting DES penetration into lignocellulose structures and accelerating the deconstruction of lignin and other components. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters, including polarity (π*), acidity (α), and basicity (β), are often used to describe the solvents and assess their solubility and dissolution behavior [38,39]. Firstly, it was found that there were certain trends in K-T parameters among DESs synthesized using CₙTAB with different chain lengths. When the alkyl chain length increased from 12 to 18, the α value of DES decreased from 1.90 to 1.02, while the β value decreased from 1.65 to 1.39, indicating a decrease in the ability of providing or receiving hydrogen bonds. Additionally, CₙTAB-based binary DESs exhibit low polarity, with π* values all below 0.1. This was related to the use of CₙTAB, which had low polarity, as a hydrogen-bond-acceptor in DES synthesis. In the presence of metal chlorides, it was manifested that the hydrogen-bond acidity and basicity of ternary DESs were elevated. The α value of TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ reached 1.87, and the β value increased to 2.08. Moreover, an increase in π* value was observed, indicating a significant enhancement in solvent polarization due to the introduction of metal ions [40] (Table S2, see supplementary materials). It was likely that the introduction of FeCl3 as an HBA in TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ strengthened the hydrogen-bond network, altered DES physicochemical properties, and enhanced the capability to better deconstruct lignocellulose.

The condensation reactions between various free furanic compounds and aromatic compounds in the system were accelerated, leading to the formation of humins and pseudo-lignin. These by-products covered the cellulose surface and hindered the binding of cellulase to catalytic sites, ultimately resulting in declined enzymatic digestion capacity [43].

In Fig. 2b and c, the influence of two factors, temperature/time and FeCl3/TTAB value, on enzymatic digestion capacity was comprehensively presented. When the pretreatment duration or temperature was fixed, the enzymatic digestion efficiency of cellulose substrate initially elevated and then dropped with an increase in the FeCl3/TTAB value. In the TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ system, FeCl3 might act as a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and interact with TTAB and lactic acid, forming complex metal cations [15]. During the pretreatment of RS, LCA as Brønsted acid and FeCl3 as Lewis acids acted synergistically, disrupting the covalent bonds in hemicellulose and lignin. This elimination of physically compacted barriers on the cellulose surface substantially enhanced cellulose accessibility. However, the existence of a large amount of FeCl3 also created conditions for the generation of inhibitors. During the pretreatment process, polymers in biomass like lignin and hemicellulose tended to break down into small molecular compounds (such as lignin monomers and furfural). These freely present small molecules underwent a series of cross-linking and condensation reactions under harsh pretreatment conditions (e.g., excessive FeCl3 existed in the system), leading to the formation of new covalent bonds and the waste of carbohydrates [44].

Due to the multitude of factors influencing pretreatment effective-ness, a more comprehensive indicator is needed to assess the intensity of pretreatment [45]. The comprehensive severity factor (CSF) is a parameter for better understanding of the influence of reaction condi-tions and chemical reactions in biomass pretreatment [45]. The rela-tionship involving delignification, xylan elimination and CSF was showcased in Fig. 3a. Most data points were encompassed within the 95 % confidence interval, and the R-squared values for the two fitted equations reached 0.93 and 0.95, respectively. As CSF increased from 2.93, the enhancement of lignin and xylan elimination was slow at first, and then gradually accelerated. When CSF exceeded about 4.5, the rate of enhancement started to slow down. This was likely due to the enhanced interaction and reaction activity between the DES and cellulose as CSF increased, leading to an accelerated pretreatment effect. As CSF further elevated, the growth of the reaction rate would become stable after the temperature reached a critical point, and the dissolution capacity of the solvent might be saturated [45].

Reusability is undoubtedly an important property of an effectual pretreatment solvent [15]. In this research, TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ was reused five times to observe its performance in lignin elimination and other aspects (Table S5, see supplementary materials). During each batch of repeated use, a part of the DES was lost, which usually occurred in the vacuum filtration step. Based on the weight of solvent before and after recycling, about 80–90 % of the solvent could be recovered per reuse. After the pretreatment, the biomass residue was separated, and the remaining TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ was reused. Upon the third reuse of the solvent, the xylan elimination declined to 65.7 %, while the lignin elimination dropped to 78.2 % (Table S5, see supplementary materials). Accordingly, the solvent manifested an apparent effect on eliminating the structures for inhibiting enzymatic hydrolysis of biomass even after multiple reuses. After five cycles of reuse, the elimination of lignin and xylan apparently declined to 62.1 % and 56.0 %, respectively (Table S5, see supplementary materials). This decrease could be attributed to the degradation of components within DES at high temperatures, leading to a reduced ability to dissolve biomass components. Additionally, in each pretreatment process, the degradation of lignin and the accumulation of other inhibitors may also lead to the decline of pretreatment performance. Consequently, the enzymatic saccharification ability of cellulose gradually diminished with each reuse. In this work, when the pretreatment efficiency of the solvent was significantly higher than that of untreated rapeseed straw (20.1 %), it could be considered to be reusable. It was observed that after three cycles of reuse, the enzymatic saccharification efficiency declined from 92.5 % to 74.1 %. After the fifth reuse, the saccharification efficiency of RS treated with TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ remained at 66.4 %, indicating the solvent's good reusability. In some published works, choline chloride (ChCl) and lactic acid (LCA) were used to synthesize a DES for the pretreatment of poplar, achieving a saccharification efficiency of 90.6 %, which still reached 51.5 % after
four reuses [49]. Switchgrass was pretreated with acidified ChCl:Gly, yielding a glucose yield of 88.9 %, which dropped to 32.6 % after three reuses [50].

Under the acidic environment, xylan can not only be hydrolyzed into a large amount of pentose units [45], but also be converted into xylo-oligosaccharides (XOSs) and furfural [20,51]. Under optimal pretreatment conditions, 3.75 g/L furfural and 3.64 g/L XOSs produced in this pretreatment liquor. As showcased in Fig. 3b, when the CSF was low, only a small amount of furfural was present in the solution due to a lower temperature. In fact, measurements revealed that almost no furfural was detected when the pretreatment temperature was 120 °C. When the CSF increased from 3.0 to 4.8, various reactions such as dehydration and isomerization of xylan-derived pentose units were promoted, leading to the synthesis of furfural and reaching a peak concentration of 3.85 g/L. As the CSF further elevated, a decrease in furfural content was observed, which was likely due to the occurrence of other side-reactions of furfural under extreme pretreatment conditions and acidic environment, leading to further condensation into humins or the generation of other byproducts [45].

During the TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ pretreatment, XOSs underwent a similar process as furfural. When the CSF was <3.5, the content of XOSs rapidly increased to approximately 5 g/L. However, as the solution environment became more severe, the content of XOSs decreased. The hydrolysis of the glycosidic bonds in its structure was accelerated, tending to degrade into its structural unit xylose or further dehydration to form furfural. However, the relationship between furfural and XOSs was not simply an antagonistic one. It was found that the rates of their side-reactions both increased under harsh treatment conditions, leading to their degradation [20]. To find mathematical models behind the data and better understand and predict the data points, a Gaussian model was used in this research to explore the relationship between CSF and furfural and XOSs yields. It could be seen that the fitted Gaussian equations well explained the relationship between CSF and the two high-value products, with R-squared values both reaching 0.95.

In addition to CSF, there also appeared to be a correlation between the CnHAB types in ternary DES and the formation of furfural and XOSs. CnHAB with different alkyl chain lengths (12–18) and lactic acid were used to synthesize DESs, and the pretreatment reaction was implemented under optimal conditions to detect the content of XOSs and furfural in the solution. Four different CnHAB with different alkyl chain lengths (12, 14, 16, and 18) were utilized for synthesizing binary DESs (Fig. 4a). The alkyl chain length of TTAB was 14. By using TTAB/LCA as pretreatment solvent, the contents of XOSs and furfural were 2.25 g/L and 2.17 g/L, respectively. As the alkyl chain length of CnHAB increased, the furfural content in the system decreased, while the XOSs content increased. This phenomenon was closely related to the non-cellulose component removal performance of different CnHAB based DESs described above. It manifested that DESs formed by CnHAB with longer alkyl chains exhibited relatively weaker xylan elimination performance, suggesting its low efficiency in the appreciation of hemicellulose.

To further understand the interactions within the DES system, an independent gradient model (IGM) analysis was performed on the MD simulation system, revealing weak interactions between cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin models, and TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (Fig. S3, see sup- plementary materials) [66]. Hydrogen bonding is a relatively strong non-covalent interaction that typically occurs between hydrogen on a strongly polar bond and an atom with a lone pair of electrons. Hemi- cellulose, being a polysaccharide rich in hydroxyl groups, could act as both a hydrogen bond donor and acceptor. As showcased in Fig. 8b, a large and dark blue region was observed and the blue scatter points had the highest density between hemicellulose and DES, implying strong hydrogen bonding interactions between them. Gromacs software was

used to calculate the intermolecular energy of the molecular dynamics simulation process from 500 ps to 10 ns, and the electrostatic energy (Eelec) between hemicellulose and TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ was calculated to be -429.3 kJ/mol, the largest among the three models (Table S6, see supplementary materials). In fact, hydrogen-bond interaction was the main form of intermolecular electric interaction, and there was a direct correlation between them, which confirmed the stronger hydrogen bond interaction between the hemicellulose model and the DES. These robust hydrogen bonds played a promoting role in the hydrolysis process of hemicellulose, aiding in the disruption of covalent bonds between sugar molecules and facilitating the generation of XOSs and furfural. The structure of lignin consists of rigid aromatic rings connected by aryl ether bonds and flexible side chains through carbon-carbon bonds, lacking strongly polar side chain groups. Consequently, the interaction types between lignin and solvents were mainly van der Waals forces instead of hydrogen bond interaction. As shown in Fig. 8c, large green areas were observed between lignin and DES, which stands for van der Waals forces. Based on intermolecular energy calculations, the lignin model is the only one in which the van der Waals (Evdw) energy (-269.46 kJ/mol) is greater than the electrostatic energy (-171.61 kJ/ mol) (Table S6, see supplementary materials). Therefore, the main force between TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ and TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ is the van der Waals interaction, which is consistent with its hydrophobic structure [21]. This explained the efficient elimination and dissolution of lignin from biomass in the TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ system. In this work, a novel surfactant-based DES system was constructed, which could realize the efficient pretreatment of RS. During the pre- treatment process, furfural, XOSs, and reducing sugars were co- produced through the effectual conversion of carbohydrates in biomass. The pretreatment of RS with ternary DES comprising CnTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3 demonstrated a promising process for biomass valorization (Fig. 11a). The interaction between Fe3+ and lactic acid (LCA) led to the formation of a "Br-lactic acid-Fe3+" supramolecular complex with the iron ion, while the ternary DES created. In this DES system, LCA provided protons for the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellu- lose and lignin, facilitating the breakdown of their complex structures.

Meanwhile, the surfactant CηTAB also played a crucial role in the pro- cess by enabling delignification and preventing pseudo-lignin re- condensation and settling on the biomass surface (Fig. 11b). Fe3+ acted as a Lewis acid catalyst, catalyzing the hydrolysis of β-1,4-glycosidic and β-O-4 linkages in hemicellulose and lignin. It underwent coordination reactions with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignin and altered its structure and properties making it more vulnerable (Fig. 11b). Although Fe3+ might inevitably undergo hydration reaction, transforming to Fe (OH)3 during the reaction, the presence of LCA in the system would greatly inhibit this conversion. These three components in DES acted synergistically to catalyze the depolymerization of lignocellulosic structures, stripping lignin and hemicellulose from RS. Quantum chemistry calculations and molecular dynamics simulations manifested that the dispersion interactions promoted the extraction and dissolution of lignin into the DES system, while hydrogen bonding interactions enhanced the reactivity between the DES and hemicellulose, improving the overall hydrolysis efficiency. To enable further high-value utili-zation, it was crucial to discuss the methods for separating these two compounds. Furfural separation technologies are primarily divided into distillation, liquid-liquid extraction, and supercritical fluid extraction [68]. Among these, distillation is the most widely used in industrial production due to its mature process and stable product quality. Liquid-liquid extraction is simple, less investment, and low energy consump-tion. Supercritical fluid extraction has low energy consumption and good separation effects but is hindered by high equipment costs. If extraction methods were to be employed, due to the complex compo-sition of the hydrolysate and the low concentration of furfural, not only would selectivity be poor, but multiple extractions might also be required, increasing production costs and energy consumption. At the same time, the application of supercritical fluid extraction is more difficult due to equipment investment and other reasons. As a result, it seems more feasible to use distillation in this work.
XOSS separation and purification technologies include chromato- graphic separation, membrane separation, and precipitation methods [69]. In this work, XOSs are present in the pretreatment liquid

containing a large amount of lignin, causing significant interference with separation and purification. Generally speaking, membrane sepa- ration technology is simple to operate with low energy consumption, strong scalability, and is suitable for industrial production applications. However, due to high equipment and membrane material costs, the initial investment is relatively high; and issues such as membrane fouling may be encountered, requiring regular maintenance. In com- parison, chromatographic separation technology offers high purity and strong selectivity, which can effectively achieve the high-purity sepa- ration of a single component of oligosaccharides in this work. The typically long operation time can also be accomplished though separa- tion equipment with higher throughput. However, the actual separation and purification technology to be adopted still needs further research based on specific production scales and expected outcomes.

4. Conclusion In this research, the novel Brønsted and Lewis acid-containing DES TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) was synthesized with TTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3. Due to the synergistic effect of the three components of DES and the complex hydrogen-bond network, TTAB/ LCA/Fe3+ showed greatly enhancement of glucose yield and effectually elimination of lignin and xylan at the optimal pretreatment conditions (162.5 °C, 61.7 min). Furthermore, co-production of furfural and XOSS was achieved through the elimination of xylan in RS. In-deep insights of RS pretreatment were given through mass balance and energy flow analysis. The physicochemical properties of DESs were studied, demonstrating its excellent properties of low viscosity, low surface tension, and strong proton donor. In this research, DESs containing Brønsted acid and Lewis acid were prepared with CₙTAB (alkyl-chain length 12–18), organic acids and metal chlorides, and the optimal treatment conditions were acquired by pretreatment optimization. Through the pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) (162.5 °C, 61.7 min), lignin (89.2 %) and xylan (77.9 %) were effectively eliminated, and the hydrophobicity of rapeseed straw substantially declined from 4.62 to 2.09 m²/g, acquiring the highest enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 92.5 %. The relationship of DES properties and enzymatic saccharification efficiency was explored. Additionally, hemicellulose in rapeseed straws could be efficiently transformed into furfural (3.75 g/L) and xylo-oligosaccharides (3.64 g/L). To clarify the structural and property changes brought by pretreatment, rapeseed straws were testified by FT-IR, SEM and CLSM and deeply discussed. The interaction between lignocellulose and TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was elucidated by molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations, explaining the effectual treatment performance and hemicel-lulose upgrading at the molecular level. Eventually, a potential pretreatment mechanism of TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was proposed. This established TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ treatment holds great promise for valorization of biomass into biofuels and biobased chemicals. 1. Introduction In the pursuit of sustainable energy, human society is actively seeking alternatives to fossil fuel consumption [1]. One promising approach is the utilization of lignocellulosic biomass, which is composed of carbohydrates (hemicellulose plus cellulose) and lignin, making it suitable for manufacturing biofuels and chemicals [2,3]. Enzymatic digestion is extensively regarded as the most promising method for utilizing carbohydrates [1]. These lignocellulose-derived reducing sugars can be further upgraded to high value-added chemicals or bio- fuels through fermentation or biocatalysis [4,5]. And these upgraded chemicals include furfural, xylo-oligosaccharides, ethanol, etc., which play an important role in the fields of resin/pharmaceutical in- termediates synthesis, health products production and energy [6]. However, the existence of lignin in lignocellulose poses challenges as they form barriers around carbohydrates, blocking the enzymatic digestion process [7]. Thus, developing an effectual pretreatment strategy for breaking down the complex structure of lignocellulosic biomass is crucial. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as effective solvents for lignocellulose treatment due to their excellent performance in enhancing enzymatic digestion [8,9]. They are a kind of readily synthesizable solvent with low vapor pressure, which can effectively separate hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. Compared with traditional hydrothermal pretreatment, it avoids the significant investment in high-pressure reactors and is less corrosive to equipment, reducing subsequent maintenance costs [10]. Typically, choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine (BA) are used as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) in DESs [11]. Besides conventional HBAs, alternative HBAs with additional functionalities for pretreatment hold significant potential to further advance pretreatment technology. As an additive with good safety and controllable costs, CₙTAB is widely used in the manufacturing of rubber and daily chemical products. Currently, the acidic CTAB:LA pretreatment strategy developed based on CTAB surfactant has shown a remarkable increase in enzyme digestibility by 72% and an improvement in cellulose accessibility from 297 mg/g to 473 mg/g [12]. Pretreatment based on CTAB-based DES has been testified to be highly beneficial as it aids in delignification and prevents the redeposition of pseudo-lignin, thereby improving cellulose accessibility and accelerating cellulose hydrolysis. In addition, the metal salt, as a kind of inexpensive and efficient Lewis acid catalysts, has attracted special attention due to its excellent pretreatment performance [13]. As a Lewis acid catalyst, metal salts can not only catalyze the hydrolysis of β-1,4-glucoside, and β-O-4 bonds in hemicellulose and lignin, but also coordinate with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignin, change their structure and chemical properties, and improve the efficiency of lignin removal. It has been widely reported to accelerate the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass, particularly hemicellulose, and to significantly improve the efficiency of biomass pretreatment. During the bulrush pretreatment, supplementary AlCl₃ could be used to assist ChCl:Gly pretreatment, acquiring high delignification (70.8%), xylan elimination (87.7%), and the saccharification yield (90.1%) [14]. Therefore, it deserves the development of new acidic DESs containing metal ion and surfactant for efficiently improving the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of lignocellulose. During the pretreatment process in acidic systems, there is also the opportunity to produce high-value products xylo-oligosaccharides (XOSs), and furfural [15], which are both important biobased addi- tives or intermediates in the food and pharmaceutical industries, with high application value [16]. It is recognized that acidic DES containing organic acids can promote the hydrolysis of hemicellulose, leading to the elevated saccharification capacity and acquiring byproducts such as xylose and XOSs. Additionally, metal chlorides, acting as Lewis acids, can favor the degradation of xylose and greatly accelerate the generation of furfural [17,18]. The protons provided by organic acids (such as lactic acid, LCA) can not only promote the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellulose and lignin, but also greatly inhibit the deactivation of metal ions due to hydration. Through the synergistic action of Brønsted acid and Lewis acid, the structure of lignocellulose is effectively disrupted, and enzy- matic hydrolysis is enhanced to obtain a high yield of reducing sugar. Moreover, this synergy facilitates the hydrolysis of xylan and dehydra- tion of xylose, promoting the formation of XOSs and furfural [15]. Supplementary of 0.2 mol/L formic acid into an aqueous system helped achieve the XOSs yield of 68% and enhance biomass saccharification ability (160 °C, 120 min) [19]. Catalyst AT-Sn-YB immobilized with Lewis acid sites (Sn⁴+) was used for the catalytic upgrading of bamboo, resulting in the production of 17.2 g/L fermentable sugars and 2.8 g/L XOSs, with an 80.3% yield of furfural [20]. To accomplish high biomass saccharification and hemicellulose utilization, the organic acid and metal chloride-containing DESs were attempted for the synthesis of XOSs, furfural and reducing sugars. To well understand the pretreatment mechanism, molecular dy- namics (MD) simulations and quantum chemistry calculations can be applied to analyze the molecular structure of lignocellulose and explore deeply the interaction between the solvent and lignocellulose. Accord- ingly, in order to further investigate the interactions between CₙTAB/ LCA/Fe³⁺ and lignocellulose at the molecular level, MD simulations and quantum chemical calculations can be attempted to deeply interpret the pretreatment mechanism combining with structural characterizations [21]. It is known that rapeseed straw (RS) represents a readily available bioenergy resource that is often disregarded and subjected to disposal or incineration practices [22,23]. It is of great interest to valorize RS into valuable chemicals through the effectual pretreatment. In this study, it was predicted that the CₙTAB-based DES pretreatment would significantly alter the physicochemical characteristics and microstructures of RS. Additionally, the increased accessibility of cellulose, and weakened hydrophobicity might be beneficial for enzymatic digestion of RS. Correspondingly, an effectual C₁TAB-based DES pretreatment process was established to address the recalcitrance of RS and mitigate the inhibitory effects of lignin and hemicellulose on enzymatic saccharification. In addition, the co-production of XOSs, furfural, and reducing sugars was developed through the efficient pretreatment. Initially, the chain length of C₁TAB (12–18), organic acid type, and metal salt type in C₁TAB-based DESs were systematically screened using single factor analysis, and the response surface method (RSM) was used to optimize the pretreatment conditions and further improve the saccharification effect of cellulose. Afterwards, the synergistic production potential of fermentable sugars, furfural, and XOSs within the pretreatment system was testified, considering factors (such as C₁TAB chain length, and FeCl₃ ratio) and their impact on pretreatment efficiency. Various analytical techniques such as FT-IR, CLSM, and SEM were employed to explore the effect of TTAB/LCA/Fe%+ on the RS morphology and properties. Molecular dynamics simulations were also utilized to gain insights into the changes in biomass properties at a molecular level. These investigations aimed to elucidate the mechanism for underlying the synergistic production and provided valuable information for the development of efficient biomass refining strategies through effectual pretreatment. ## 2. The impacts of different C_nTAB, organic acid and metal chloride in DES were examined on the changes of glucose yield and RS components (Fig. 1). Fig. 1a showcased that the glucose yield from biomass didn't increase consistently as the chain length of C_nTAB increased from 12 to 18. It manifested that the tetra- decyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB)-based DES obtained the best pretreatment effectiveness, acquiring an enzymatic digestion efficiency of 64.5 %. As illustrated in Fig. 1e, it could be observed that xylan and lignin in the biomass was significant eliminated as the chain length of C_nTAB decreased, increasing the xylan elimination from 65.5 % to 73.4 % and delignification from 61.8 % to 77.4 % (Table S1, see supple- mentary materials). After pretreatment with DTAB/LCA, the solid re- covery was <40 %, which was the lowest among all the C_nTAB-based DESs tested. It turned out that the DTAB resulted in the most significant structural disruption. However, although the dodecyl- trimethylammonium bromide (DTAB) with the shortest alkyl chains exhibited the most significant structural disruption based on chemical composition, it didn't acquire the best glucose yield. This was likely due to the higher production of inhibitory compounds during the more intense pretreatment process caused by DTAB, thereby limiting the saccharification efficiency of RS [32]. The Brønsted acid in the ternary DES played a crucial role in biomass pretreatment by providing a large number of protons for attacking the chemical bonds in biomass, thus substantially reducing the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials [19]. In this research, four different mono- carboxylic acids with varying chain lengths and two common organic acids (lactic acid and levulinic acid) were individually mixed with the best CₙTAB obtained above, and TTAB-based DESs with different organic acids were screened to acquire the most suitable binary CₙTAB- based DES for RS pretreatment. From Fig. 1f, the RS treated with DES containing lactic acid (LCA) had the lowest lignin content (9.4%). It could be calculated that DES containing LCA effectually eliminated the highest amount of lignin (77.2%) and xylan (69.7%) within the system, followed by the DES with formic acid, reaching 74.9% and 76.8%, respectively. Among these organic acids, butyric acid exhibited the weakest disruption of the lignocellulose structure, which might be attributed to its relatively higher pKa value. Fig. 1b indicated that the RS pretreatment using CnHAB-based DES containing LCA exhibited the best performance, with an enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 64.5 %. Additionally, it was observed that the elimination capacity of monocarboxylic acids for lignin and xylan gradually weakened with increasing chain length. This trend was closely related to the pKa values, as showcased in Fig. 1b. As the chain length of monocarboxylic acids increased, their pKa values also rose, resulting in a decline in pretreatment efficiency. However, the pKa of acids couldn't be used directly to predict pretreatment results. When organic acids such as lactic acid possess more complex structures, including hydroxyl and carbonyl groups, the correlation between pKa and pretreatment performance couldn't be simply described as negative. On one hand, different functional groups apparently influenced the stereostructure of organic acids, thereby affecting the pretreatment process. On the other hand, complex organic acids might exhibit intramolecular interactions, such as the significant impact of hydroxyl groups on hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic interactions, which would influence the ionization equilibrium of carboxyl groups. In the pretreatment system, metal chlorides can not only act as Lewis acid to catalyze the hydrolysis of chemical bonds such as β-1,4-glucoside and β-O-4 bonds in hemicelluloses and lignin [33], but also react with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignocellulose to form metal ion-lignin complexes, making them easier to degrade [13]. In Fig. 1c, the pretreatment effectiveness of nine DESs containing different metal chlorides was compared. It was manifested that the ternary DESs containing metal chlorides exhibited apparently improved pretreatment performance compared to TTAB/LCA. The lowest enzymatic digestion efficiency for RS pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Mn²⁺ was 54.3 %, while higher saccharification efficiencies were acquired with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ and TTAB/LCA/Al³⁺ treatments, reaching 83.6 % and 81.5 %, respectively. Considering the comprehensive screening of components in the ternary DES above, TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was considered the optimal CₙTAB-based ternary DES for RS pretreatment. It is widely recognized that the properties of DESs have substantial impacts on the elimination of biomass components [34]. As shown in the FT-IR image of TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (Fig. S1, see supplementary materials), 4 Z. Tang et al. International Journal of Biological Macromolecules 301 (2025) 140151 a peak due to the stretching vibration of -OH was observed at 3450 cm⁻¹, showing a blue shift compared to LCA, indicating the formation of a new hydrogen bond network in DES [35]. The peak appeared at 1746 cm⁻¹ was associated with C=O in from LCA [36]. A peak at 966 cm⁻¹ was attributed to the C–N group of TTAB and the absorption around 744 cm⁻¹ was connected with Fe³⁺-OH- Fe³⁺ [37]. In biomass pretreatment, solvent viscosity plays a crucial role in the diffusion rate of molecules [34]. There was a substantial difference in viscosity among DESs synthesized using CₙTAB with different chain lengths (Table S2, see supplementary materials). It was evident that DESs synthesized with shorter alkyl chain lengths exhibit lower viscosity. The viscosity of octadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (OTAB) was 1983.5 cp, while that of DTAB was only 350.3 cp. It was probably related to lower intermolecular friction caused by lower chain length, thus resulting in better mobility. This helped the molecules move more easily in the solvent, confirming that TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ had better pretreatment performance. Additionally, at room temperature, ternary DESs showed a significant reduction in viscosity compared to binary DESs. The viscosity of TTAB/LCA reached 848.2 cp, whereas TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ had only 674.2 cp. These findings regarding viscosity were consistent with previous studies on the pretreatment effectiveness of different DESs. Surface tension is also a crucial solvent property known to influence the pretreatment process. Solvents with low surface tension might better interact with biomass and rapidly penetrate structures such as lignin. The formed stronger interactions would facilitate their efficient removal. TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ had a surface tension of only 30.2 mN/m (Table S2, see supplementary materials). In comparison, the surface tension of water was 72 mN/m (25 °C), significantly higher than that of this efficient pretreatment solvent. Consistent with the viscosity trend, the shorter chain lengths of CₙTAB also contributed to lower surface tension in DESs, thereby promoting DES penetration into lignocellulose structures and accelerating the deconstruction of lignin and other components. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters, including polarity (π*), acidity (α), and basicity (β), are often used to describe the solvents and assess their solubility and dissolution behavior [38,39]. Firstly, it was found that there were certain trends in K-T parameters among DESs synthesized using CₙTAB with different chain lengths. When the alkyl chain length increased from 12 to 18, the α value of DES decreased from 1.90 to 1.02, while the β value decreased from 1.65 to 1.39, indicating a decrease in the ability of providing or receiving hydrogen bonds. Additionally, CₙTAB-based binary DESs exhibit low polarity, with π* values all below 0.1. This was related to the use of CₙTAB, which had low polarity, as a hydrogen-bond-acceptor in DES synthesis. In the presence of metal chlorides, it was manifested that the hydrogen-bond acidity and basicity of ternary DESs were elevated. In this work, a novel surfactant-based DES system was constructed, which could realize the efficient pretreatment of RS. The pretreatment of RS with ternary DES comprising CnTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3 demonstrated a promising process for biomass valorization (Fig. 11a). The interaction between Fe3+ and lactic acid (LCA) led to the formation of a "Br-lactic acid-Fe3+" supramolecular complex with the iron ion, while the ternary DES created. In this DES system, LCA provided protons for the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellu- lose and lignin, facilitating the breakdown of their complex structures. Meanwhile, the surfactant CηTAB also played a crucial role in the pro- cess by enabling delignification and preventing pseudo-lignin re- condensation and settling on the biomass surface (Fig. 11b). It underwent coordination reactions with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignin and altered its structure and properties making it more vulnerable (Fig. 11b). Although Fe3+ might inevitably undergo hydration reaction, transforming to Fe (OH)3 during the reaction, the presence of LCA in the system would greatly inhibit this conversion. These three components in DES acted synergistically to catalyze the depolymerization of lignocellulosic structures, stripping lignin and hemicellulose from RS. To enable further high-value utili-zation, it was crucial to discuss the methods for separating these two compounds. Furfural separation technologies are primarily divided into distillation, liquid-liquid extraction, and supercritical fluid extraction [68]. Among these, distillation is the most widely used in industrial production due to its mature process and stable product quality. Liquid-liquid extraction is simple, less investment, and low energy consump-tion. Supercritical fluid extraction has low energy consumption and good separation effects but is hindered by high equipment costs. If extraction methods were to be employed, due to the complex compo-sition of the hydrolysate and the low concentration of furfural, not only would selectivity be poor, but multiple extractions might also be required, increasing production costs and energy consumption. At the same time, the application of supercritical fluid extraction is more difficult due to equipment investment and other reasons. As a result, it seems more feasible to use distillation in this work. XOSS separation and purification technologies include chromato- graphic separation, membrane separation, and precipitation methods [69]. In this work, XOSs are present in the pretreatment liquid containing a large amount of lignin, causing significant interference with separation and purification. Generally speaking, membrane sepa- ration technology is simple to operate with low energy consumption, strong scalability, and is suitable for industrial production applications. However, due to high equipment and membrane material costs, the initial investment is relatively high; and issues such as membrane fouling may be encountered, requiring regular maintenance. In com- parison, chromatographic separation technology offers high purity and strong selectivity, which can effectively achieve the high-purity sepa- ration of a single component of oligosaccharides in this work. The typically long operation time can also be accomplished though separa- tion equipment with higher throughput. However, the actual separation and purification technology to be adopted still needs further research based on specific production scales and expected outcomes. 4. Conclusion In this research, the novel Brønsted and Lewis acid-containing DES TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) was synthesized with TTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3. Due to the synergistic effect of the three components of DES and the complex hydrogen-bond network, TTAB/ LCA/Fe3+ showed greatly enhancement of glucose yield and effectually elimination of lignin and xylan at the optimal pretreatment conditions (162.5 °C, 61.7 min). Furthermore, co-production of furfural and XOSS was achieved through the elimination of xylan in RS. In-deep insights of RS pretreatment were given through mass balance and energy flow analysis. The physicochemical properties of DESs were studied, demonstrating its excellent properties of low viscosity, low surface tension, and strong proton donor. In this research, DESs containing Brønsted acid and Lewis acid were prepared with CₙTAB (alkyl-chain length 12–18), organic acids and metal chlorides, and the optimal treatment conditions were acquired by pretreatment optimization. Through the pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) (162.5 °C, 61.7 min), lignin (89.2 %) and xylan (77.9 %) were effectively eliminated, and the hydrophobicity of rapeseed straw substantially declined from 4.62 to 2.09 m²/g, acquiring the highest enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 92.5 %. The relationship of DES properties and enzymatic saccharification efficiency was explored. Additionally, hemicellulose in rapeseed straws could be efficiently transformed into furfural (3.75 g/L) and xylo-oligosaccharides (3.64 g/L). To clarify the structural and property changes brought by pretreatment, rapeseed straws were testified by FT-IR, SEM and CLSM and deeply discussed. The interaction between lignocellulose and TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was elucidated by molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemical calculations, explaining the effectual treatment performance and hemicel-lulose upgrading at the molecular level. Eventually, a potential pretreatment mechanism of TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was proposed. This established TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ treatment holds great promise for valorization of biomass into biofuels and biobased chemicals. 1. Introduction In the pursuit of sustainable energy, human society is actively seeking alternatives to fossil fuel consumption [1]. One promising approach is the utilization of lignocellulosic biomass, which is composed of carbohydrates (hemicellulose plus cellulose) and lignin, making it suitable for manufacturing biofuels and chemicals [2,3]. Enzymatic digestion is extensively regarded as the most promising method for utilizing carbohydrates [1]. These lignocellulose-derived reducing sugars can be further upgraded to high value-added chemicals or bio- fuels through fermentation or biocatalysis [4,5]. And these upgraded chemicals include furfural, xylo-oligosaccharides, ethanol, etc., which play an important role in the fields of resin/pharmaceutical in- termediates synthesis, health products production and energy [6]. However, the existence of lignin in lignocellulose poses challenges as they form barriers around carbohydrates, blocking the enzymatic digestion process [7]. Thus, developing an effectual pretreatment strategy for breaking down the complex structure of lignocellulosic biomass is crucial. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as effective solvents for lignocellulose treatment due to their excellent performance in enhancing enzymatic digestion [8,9]. They are a kind of readily synthesizable solvent with low vapor pressure, which can effectively separate hemicellulose and lignin from biomass. Compared with traditional hydrothermal pretreatment, it avoids the significant investment in high-pressure reactors and is less corrosive to equipment, reducing subsequent maintenance costs [10]. Typically, choline chloride (ChCl) and betaine (BA) are used as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) in DESs [11]. Besides conventional HBAs, alternative HBAs with additional functionalities for pretreatment hold significant potential to further advance pretreatment technology. As an additive with good safety and controllable costs, CₙTAB is widely used in the manufacturing of rubber and daily chemical products. Currently, the acidic CTAB:LA pretreatment strategy developed based on CTAB surfactant has shown a remarkable increase in enzyme digestibility by 72% and an improvement in cellulose accessibility from 297 mg/g to 473 mg/g [12]. Pretreatment based on CTAB-based DES has been testified to be highly beneficial as it aids in delignification and prevents the redeposition of pseudo-lignin, thereby improving cellulose accessibility and accelerating cellulose hydrolysis. In addition, the metal salt, as a kind of inexpensive and efficient Lewis acid catalysts, has attracted special attention due to its excellent pretreatment performance [13]. As a Lewis acid catalyst, metal salts can not only catalyze the hydrolysis of β-1,4-glucoside, and β-O-4 bonds in hemicellulose and lignin, but also coordinate with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignin, change their structure and chemical properties, and improve the efficiency of lignin removal. It has been widely reported to accelerate the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass, particularly hemicellulose, and to significantly improve the efficiency of biomass pretreatment. During the bulrush pretreatment, supplementary AlCl₃ could be used to assist ChCl:Gly pretreatment, acquiring high delignification (70.8%), xylan elimination (87.7%), and the saccharification yield (90.1%) [14]. Therefore, it deserves the development of new acidic DESs containing metal ion and surfactant for efficiently improving the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of lignocellulose. During the pretreatment process in acidic systems, there is also the opportunity to produce high-value products xylo-oligosaccharides (XOSs), and furfural [15], which are both important biobased addi- tives or intermediates in the food and pharmaceutical industries, with high application value [16]. It is recognized that acidic DES containing organic acids can promote the hydrolysis of hemicellulose, leading to the elevated saccharification capacity and acquiring byproducts such as xylose and XOSs. Additionally, metal chlorides, acting as Lewis acids, can favor the degradation of xylose and greatly accelerate the generation of furfural [17,18]. The protons provided by organic acids (such as lactic acid, LCA) can not only promote the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellulose and lignin, but also greatly inhibit the deactivation of metal ions due to hydration. Through the synergistic action of Brønsted acid and Lewis acid, the structure of lignocellulose is effectively disrupted, and enzy- matic hydrolysis is enhanced to obtain a high yield of reducing sugar. Moreover, this synergy facilitates the hydrolysis of xylan and dehydra- tion of xylose, promoting the formation of XOSs and furfural [15]. Supplementary of 0.2 mol/L formic acid into an aqueous system helped achieve the XOSs yield of 68% and enhance biomass saccharification ability (160 °C, 120 min) [19]. Catalyst AT-Sn-YB immobilized with Lewis acid sites (Sn⁴+) was used for the catalytic upgrading of bamboo, resulting in the production of 17.2 g/L fermentable sugars and 2.8 g/L XOSs, with an 80.3% yield of furfural [20]. To accomplish high biomass saccharification and hemicellulose utilization, the organic acid and metal chloride-containing DESs were attempted for the synthesis of XOSs, furfural and reducing sugars. To well understand the pretreatment mechanism, molecular dy- namics (MD) simulations and quantum chemistry calculations can be applied to analyze the molecular structure of lignocellulose and explore deeply the interaction between the solvent and lignocellulose. Accord- ingly, in order to further investigate the interactions between CₙTAB/ LCA/Fe³⁺ and lignocellulose at the molecular level, MD simulations and quantum chemical calculations can be attempted to deeply interpret the pretreatment mechanism combining with structural characterizations [21]. It is known that rapeseed straw (RS) represents a readily available bioenergy resource that is often disregarded and subjected to disposal or incineration practices [22,23]. It is of great interest to valorize RS into valuable chemicals through the effectual pretreatment. In this study, it was predicted that the CₙTAB-based DES pretreatment would significantly alter the physicochemical characteristics and microstructures of RS. Additionally, the increased accessibility of cellulose, and weakened hydrophobicity might be beneficial for enzymatic digestion of RS. Correspondingly, an effectual C₁TAB-based DES pretreatment process was established to address the recalcitrance of RS and mitigate the inhibitory effects of lignin and hemicellulose on enzymatic saccharification. In addition, the co-production of XOSs, furfural, and reducing sugars was developed through the efficient pretreatment. Initially, the chain length of C₁TAB (12–18), organic acid type, and metal salt type in C₁TAB-based DESs were systematically screened using single factor analysis, and the response surface method (RSM) was used to optimize the pretreatment conditions and further improve the saccharification effect of cellulose. Afterwards, the synergistic production potential of fermentable sugars, furfural, and XOSs within the pretreatment system was testified, considering factors (such as C₁TAB chain length, and FeCl₃ ratio) and their impact on pretreatment efficiency. Various analytical techniques such as FT-IR, CLSM, and SEM were employed to explore the effect of TTAB/LCA/Fe%+ on the RS morphology and properties. Molecular dynamics simulations were also utilized to gain insights into the changes in biomass properties at a molecular level. These investigations aimed to elucidate the mechanism for underlying the synergistic production and provided valuable information for the development of efficient biomass refining strategies through effectual pretreatment. ## 2. The impacts of different C_nTAB, organic acid and metal chloride in DES were examined on the changes of glucose yield and RS components (Fig. 1). Fig. 1a showcased that the glucose yield from biomass didn't increase consistently as the chain length of C_nTAB increased from 12 to 18. It manifested that the tetra- decyltrimethylammonium bromide (TTAB)-based DES obtained the best pretreatment effectiveness, acquiring an enzymatic digestion efficiency of 64.5 %. As illustrated in Fig. 1e, it could be observed that xylan and lignin in the biomass was significant eliminated as the chain length of C_nTAB decreased, increasing the xylan elimination from 65.5 % to 73.4 % and delignification from 61.8 % to 77.4 % (Table S1, see supple- mentary materials). After pretreatment with DTAB/LCA, the solid re- covery was <40 %, which was the lowest among all the C_nTAB-based DESs tested. It turned out that the DTAB resulted in the most significant structural disruption. However, although the dodecyl- trimethylammonium bromide (DTAB) with the shortest alkyl chains exhibited the most significant structural disruption based on chemical composition, it didn't acquire the best glucose yield. This was likely due to the higher production of inhibitory compounds during the more intense pretreatment process caused by DTAB, thereby limiting the saccharification efficiency of RS [32]. The Brønsted acid in the ternary DES played a crucial role in biomass pretreatment by providing a large number of protons for attacking the chemical bonds in biomass, thus substantially reducing the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic materials [19]. In this research, four different mono- carboxylic acids with varying chain lengths and two common organic acids (lactic acid and levulinic acid) were individually mixed with the best CₙTAB obtained above, and TTAB-based DESs with different organic acids were screened to acquire the most suitable binary CₙTAB- based DES for RS pretreatment. From Fig. 1f, the RS treated with DES containing lactic acid (LCA) had the lowest lignin content (9.4%). It could be calculated that DES containing LCA effectually eliminated the highest amount of lignin (77.2%) and xylan (69.7%) within the system, followed by the DES with formic acid, reaching 74.9% and 76.8%, respectively. Among these organic acids, butyric acid exhibited the weakest disruption of the lignocellulose structure, which might be attributed to its relatively higher pKa value. Fig. 1b indicated that the RS pretreatment using CnHAB-based DES containing LCA exhibited the best performance, with an enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 64.5 %. Additionally, it was observed that the elimination capacity of monocarboxylic acids for lignin and xylan gradually weakened with increasing chain length. This trend was closely related to the pKa values, as showcased in Fig. 1b. As the chain length of monocarboxylic acids increased, their pKa values also rose, resulting in a decline in pretreatment efficiency. However, the pKa of acids couldn't be used directly to predict pretreatment results. When organic acids such as lactic acid possess more complex structures, including hydroxyl and carbonyl groups, the correlation between pKa and pretreatment performance couldn't be simply described as negative. On one hand, different functional groups apparently influenced the stereostructure of organic acids, thereby affecting the pretreatment process. On the other hand, complex organic acids might exhibit intramolecular interactions, such as the significant impact of hydroxyl groups on hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic interactions, which would influence the ionization equilibrium of carboxyl groups. In the pretreatment system, metal chlorides can not only act as Lewis acid to catalyze the hydrolysis of chemical bonds such as β-1,4-glucoside and β-O-4 bonds in hemicelluloses and lignin [33], but also react with hydroxyl and phenolic groups in lignocellulose to form metal ion-lignin complexes, making them easier to degrade [13]. In Fig. 1c, the pretreatment effectiveness of nine DESs containing different metal chlorides was compared. It was manifested that the ternary DESs containing metal chlorides exhibited apparently improved pretreatment performance compared to TTAB/LCA. The lowest enzymatic digestion efficiency for RS pretreatment with TTAB/LCA/Mn²⁺ was 54.3 %, while higher saccharification efficiencies were acquired with TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ and TTAB/LCA/Al³⁺ treatments, reaching 83.6 % and 81.5 %, respectively. Considering the comprehensive screening of components in the ternary DES above, TTAB/LCA/Fe³⁺ was considered the optimal CₙTAB-based ternary DES for RS pretreatment. A peak at 966 cm⁻¹ was attributed to the C–N group of TTAB and the absorption around 744 cm⁻¹ was connected with Fe³⁺-OH- Fe³⁺ [37]. There was a substantial difference in viscosity among DESs synthesized using CₙTAB with different chain lengths (Table S2, see supplementary materials). In the initial state, 1000 g raw RS contained 301.6 g glucan, 151.4 g xylan, and 189.0 g lignin. The pretreatment of RS with ternary DES comprising CnTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3 demonstrated a promising process for biomass valorization (Fig. 11a). The interaction between Fe3+ and lactic acid (LCA) led to the formation of a "Br-lactic acid-Fe3+" supramolecular complex with the iron ion, while the ternary DES created. In this DES system, LCA provided protons for the efficient hydrolysis of hemicellu- lose and lignin, facilitating the breakdown of their complex structures. Meanwhile, the surfactant CηTAB also played a crucial role in the pro- cess by enabling delignification and preventing pseudo-lignin re- condensation and settling on the biomass surface (Fig. 11b). Although Fe3+ might inevitably undergo hydration reaction, transforming to Fe (OH)3 during the reaction, the presence of LCA in the system would greatly inhibit this conversion. These three components in DES acted synergistically to catalyze the depolymerization of lignocellulosic structures, stripping lignin and hemicellulose from RS. To enable further high-value utili-zation, it was crucial to discuss the methods for separating these two compounds. Furfural separation technologies are primarily divided into distillation, liquid-liquid extraction, and supercritical fluid extraction [68]. Among these, distillation is the most widely used in industrial production due to its mature process and stable product quality. Liquid-liquid extraction is simple, less investment, and low energy consump-tion. Supercritical fluid extraction has low energy consumption and good separation effects but is hindered by high equipment costs. If extraction methods were to be employed, due to the complex compo-sition of the hydrolysate and the low concentration of furfural, not only would selectivity be poor, but multiple extractions might also be required, increasing production costs and energy consumption. At the same time, the application of supercritical fluid extraction is more difficult due to equipment investment and other reasons. As a result, it seems more feasible to use distillation in this work. XOSS separation and purification technologies include chromato- graphic separation, membrane separation, and precipitation methods [69]. In this work, XOSs are present in the pretreatment liquid containing a large amount of lignin, causing significant interference with separation and purification. Generally speaking, membrane sepa- ration technology is simple to operate with low energy consumption, strong scalability, and is suitable for industrial production applications. However, due to high equipment and membrane material costs, the initial investment is relatively high; and issues such as membrane fouling may be encountered, requiring regular maintenance. In com- parison, chromatographic separation technology offers high purity and strong selectivity, which can effectively achieve the high-purity sepa- ration of a single component of oligosaccharides in this work. The typically long operation time can also be accomplished though separa- tion equipment with higher throughput. However, the actual separation and purification technology to be adopted still needs further research based on specific production scales and expected outcomes. 4. Conclusion In this research, the novel Brønsted and Lewis acid-containing DES TTAB/LCA/Fe3+ (1:4:0.0111, mol:mol:mol) was synthesized with TTAB, lactic acid, and FeCl3. The physicochemical properties of DESs were studied, demonstrating its excellent properties of low viscosity, low surface tension, and strong proton donor.
